title: What does the Queensland Food Act 2006 require of a food safety supervisor?
description: Queensland Food Act 2006 sections 86 to 88: when a licensee must have a food safety supervisor, what the role requires, council notice deadlines, penalties.
shortAnswer: Under sections 86 to 88 of the Queensland Food Act 2006, a holder of a food business license must have a food safety supervisor within 30 days after the license is issued and at all times afterwards, keep that supervisor reasonably available to the local government and to food handlers, and notify the council of each supervisor's name and contact details. Each failure carries a maximum of 50 penalty units, and executive officers can be personally liable.
keyTakeaways: Section 86(1) requires a licensee to have a food safety supervisor within 30 days after the license is issued under section 60(1); section 86(2) requires one at all times afterwards.
Section 87 requires the supervisor to be reasonably available to be contacted by the local government and by food handlers while the business operates.
Section 88 requires notice to the council of each supervisor's details within 30 days of licensing, and within 14 days of any appointment, departure or change of contact details.

The Act defines a food safety supervisor by competence: knowing how to recognize, prevent and alleviate the business's food safety hazards, with relevant skills, knowledge and authority to direct handlers.
Category one and two businesses must also meet Standard 3.2.2A, which requires the supervisor's certificate to have been obtained within the past five years.
jurisdiction: Australia (Queensland): Food Act 2006 (Qld), chapter 3, part 7, division 2
regulator: Queensland Health (administering agency) and local governments, which license and inspect food businesses
appliesTo: Licensable food businesses that manufacture food
For profit businesses selling unpackaged food by retail, such as restaurants, delicatessens, caterers, takeaway shops, motels supplying meals and mobile food vans
Non-profit organizations selling meals prepared at a particular place on at least 12 days each financial year
Licensees, including executive officers of corporate licensees

sections.heading: Which Queensland businesses need a food safety supervisor?

blocks.text: Every holder of a license for a licensable food business needs a food safety supervisor. Section 48 of the [Food Act 2006](https://www.legislation.qld.gov.au/view/whole/html/inforce/current/act-2006-003) defines a licensable food business as one that manufactures food, a for profit business selling unpackaged food by retail, or a non-profit organization selling meals it prepares at a particular place on at least 12 days each financial year.

The Act's examples include a restaurant or delicatessen, a catering business, a takeaway pizza shop, a motel supplying meals with accommodation, and a business selling hamburgers from a motor vehicle. Section 48(2) excludes businesses that only sell unpackaged snack food, whole fruit or vegetables, drinks other than juice processed at the point of sale, ice, or seeds, spices, tea and coffee beans.

That drinks exclusion means a bar that only pours drinks is not a licensable food business under the Food Act merely because it sells alcohol; it becomes one when it sells unpackaged food by retail. Liquor obligations are separate, as the [NSW RSA](/regulations/responsible-service-of-alcohol-training-nsw) and [Victorian RSA](/regulations/responsible-service-of-alcohol-training-victoria) pages show for those states.

sections.heading: What do sections 86 to 88 require of the licensee?

blocks.text: The three sections place the duty on the licensee, not on the supervisor. The licensee must appoint, keep available and notify; the supervisor's own role is defined by the competence the Act expects.

blocks.text: Section 86(3) allows the licensee to be the food safety supervisor and to have more than one. The notes to sections 86(1) and 86(2) state that if a corporation commits the offense, each executive officer may be taken under section 260A to have also committed it, which makes supervisor coverage a director level compliance item.

sections.heading: What must a Queensland food safety supervisor know?

blocks.text: The Act sets a competence test rather than naming a course. Schedule 3 defines a food safety supervisor as a person who knows how to recognize, prevent and alleviate the food safety hazards of the business, has skills and knowledge in food safety relevant to the business, and has authority to supervise and give directions about food safety to the people who handle food.

blocks.title: Primary text: Food Act 2006 (Qld), schedule 3
blocks.text: "food safety supervisor, for a food business, means a person who (a) knows how to recognise, prevent and alleviate food safety hazards of the food business; and (b) has skills and knowledge in matters relating to food safety relevant to the food business; and (c) has the authority to supervise and give directions about matters relating to food safety to persons who handle food in the food business."

The phrase "of the food business" matters. A supervisor certificate from a generic course is evidence of skills and knowledge, but an inspector can also test whether the supervisor understands the hazards of this kitchen's menu and processes. Section 262(2)(f) allows the chief executive of Queensland Health to make guidelines about the skills and knowledge required for a person to be a food safety supervisor.

sections.heading: How does Standard 3.2.2A change the Queensland requirement?

blocks.text: For category one and category two businesses, Standard 3.2.2A of the Food Standards Code adds a certificate rule on top of the Queensland Act. [Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ)](https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/food-safety/food-safety-supervisor) says the certificate must have been obtained within the past 5 years and must come from a registered training organization or an organization recognized by the relevant food regulator.

FSANZ also says reasonably available means the supervisor works on site and oversees handling of high risk unpackaged food, or can be easily contacted, for example by phone. Queensland's section 87 adds a second audience: the supervisor must be contactable by the local government as well as by food handlers. The [Standard 3.2.2A page](/regulations/food-safety-standard-3-2-2a-training) covers the national rules, including food handler training, in full.

sections.heading: What evidence should a Queensland licensee keep?

blocks.text: A licensee should be able to show, on any day, who the supervisor is, that the council has been told, and that the supervisor's competence is current. The table is an illustrative template combining the Act and Standard 3.2.2A.

blocks.text: Because each change of supervisor starts a 14 day clock, staff turnover in a kitchen is a compliance event, not only a rostering one. Building the trigger into offboarding is covered in [how to structure onboarding for regulated roles](/guides/how-to-structure-onboarding-for-regulated-roles), and site specific checks can use a [competency assessment](/glossary/competency-assessment).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models the schedule 3 definition as three assessable outcomes tied to each site's hazards, so a supervisor's competence is evidenced against the actual menu and process, not just a course certificate. Supervisor changes can trigger a notice task for the licensee. See [operational procedure programs](/programs/operational-procedures).

faqs.q: Can the licensee be the food safety supervisor in Queensland?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 86(3) of the Food Act 2006 says the licensee may be the food safety supervisor and may have more than one supervisor. Having several supervisors helps meet the section 87 duty to keep one reasonably available whenever the business is trading.

faqs.q: How long does a Queensland licensee have to notify council of a new supervisor?
faqs.a: For the first supervisor, 30 days after the license is issued under section 60(1). After that, section 88 requires notice within 14 days when someone becomes or stops being a supervisor, or when a supervisor's contact details change. Each failure carries a maximum of 50 penalty units.

faqs.q: Does a Queensland food safety supervisor certificate expire?
faqs.a: The Queensland Act itself does not set an expiry period. For category one and category two businesses, Standard 3.2.2A requires the supervisor's certificate to have been obtained within the past five years, so in practice most food service and retail supervisors renew every five years.

faqs.q: Does a non-profit sausage sizzle need a food safety supervisor?
faqs.a: Usually not. A non-profit is a licensable food business only if it sells meals it prepares at a particular place on at least 12 days each financial year. Occasional fundraising events below that threshold fall outside the licensing and supervisor provisions, though general food safety duties still apply.
